claims.text: The initial alloy is equal-atomic NbMoTaW with a single BCC phase.
Equal-atomic BCC NbMoTaW has excellent high-temperature mechanical properties.
Equal-atomic BCC NbMoTaW has limited room-temperature ductility.
The irradiation tolerance of the initial NbMoTaW alloy is experimentally unverified.
The proposed intervention is to add approximately 5 at% V to NbMoTaW by arc melting, followed by controlled cooling and extended homogenization.
The proposed composition and processing will form a fine, uniform dispersion of coherent nanoscale V-rich precipitates in the BCC matrix.
The proposed processing will modify grain-boundary structures so that they act as efficient defect sinks.
Vanadium has a lower melting point than the principal constituents of NbMoTaW.
Vanadium is inherently more ductile than the initial NbMoTaW alloy.
Vanadium addition will produce local lattice distortions that facilitate dislocation mobility.
Facilitated dislocation mobility will improve room-temperature ductility.
Coherent V-rich precipitates will act as sinks for irradiation-induced defects and helium atoms.
Defect and helium trapping at the precipitates will promote defect recombination and reduce helium-bubble formation and blistering.
The precipitate-mediated irradiation response will not compromise the high-temperature integrity of the BCC matrix.
Relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the V-modified alloy will show a 20–30% increase in room-temperature ductility.
Relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the V-modified alloy will maintain comparable strength at 1600 °C.
The V-modified alloy will exhibit reduced helium-bubble formation and blistering relative to untreated NbMoTaW.
The V-modified alloy will exhibit less irradiation-induced phase instability than untreated NbMoTaW.
In situ TEM will reveal uniform, coherent V-rich precipitates functioning as defect sinks.
The stated irradiation-tolerance prediction is bounded to helium-ion energies of 50–500 keV at dose rates approximating reactor conditions.
